# MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination

Zhuo Li^(∗†) Affiliation: Qwen Large Model Application Team, Alibaba

Zhang^(∗) Affiliation: Qwen Large Model Application Team, Alibaba

###### Abstract

Hallucination remains a critical bottleneck for large language models
(LLMs), undermining their reliability in real-world applications,
especially in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. While
existing hallucination detection methods employ LLM-as-a-judge to verify
LLM outputs against retrieved evidence, they suffer from inherent
confirmation bias, where the verifier inadvertently reproduces the
errors of the original generation. To address this, we introduce
Multi-Agent Reinforced self-Check for Hallucination (MARCH), a framework
that enforces rigorous factual alignment by leveraging deliberate
information asymmetry. MARCH orchestrates a collaborative pipeline of
three specialized agents: a Solver, a Proposer, and a Checker. The
Solver generates an initial RAG response, which the Proposer decomposes
into claim-level verifiable atomic propositions. Crucially, the Checker
validates these propositions against retrieved evidence in isolation,
deprived of the Solver’s original output. This well-crafted information
asymmetry scheme breaks the cycle of self-confirmation bias. By training
this pipeline with multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), we enable
the agents to co-evolve and optimize factual adherence. Extensive
experiments across hallucination benchmarks demonstrate that MARCH
substantially reduces hallucination rates. Notably, an 8B-parameter LLM
equipped with MARCH achieves performance competitive with powerful
closed-source models. MARCH paves a scalable path for factual
self-improvement of LLMs through co-evolution. The code is at
[https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/MARCH](https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/MARCH).

![Refer to caption](2603.24579v1/figures/march-framework-v3.png)

Figure 1: Overview of the MARCH framework. The Solver conducts
retrieval-augmented generation base on the input query and related
documents. The Proposer then decomposes this response into atomic
propositions (the orange line in the response block) and formulates
verifiable question-answer pairs. The Checker performs isolated
verification by re-answering questions solely based on the retrieved
evidence, without access to the Solver’s original output. This
information-asymmetric pipeline, where the policy model plays all three
roles, is optimized via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to
achieve robust factual alignment.

## 1 Introduction

Despite the remarkable success achieved by Large Language Models (LLMs)
([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib8); [Touvron et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Yang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib9); [DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib6); [Gemini,
2025](#bib.bib72)), the persistence of _hallucinations_ remains a
fundamental barrier to LLMs’ trustworthy usage ([Kalai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11); [Ji et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13); [Maynez et al., 2020](#bib.bib74)). Even enhanced
within Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib14)), LLMs frequently generate responses that, while
linguistically fluent, contradict the provided evidentiary context ([Xu
et al., 2025c](#bib.bib12)). Such context-conflicting hallucinations
([Liu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib15)) are particularly prevalent in
data-intensive tasks, manifesting as inaccurate numbers, distorted
temporal sequences, or erroneous arithmetic aggregations, even when the
source text explicitly contains the requisite information. In
high-stakes domains, such as finance ([Kang and Liu, 2023](#bib.bib24)),
law ([Dahl et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)), and healthcare ([Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)), hallucinations are more prohibitive, as users
require LLMs to function as meticulous evidence readers rather than
creative generators of plausible but unverified narratives.

Among approaches in mitigating hallucinations, Supervised Fine-Tune
(SFT) has been primarily considered as effective ([Elaraby et al.,
2023](#bib.bib61); [Lin et al., 2022](#bib.bib60); [Zhou et al.,
2023](#bib.bib59)). However, several practices emphasize that SFT could
also amplify hallucinations by fundamentally operating on behavior
cloning ([Torabi et al., 2018](#bib.bib62)), which induces models to
prioritize authoritative stylistic patterns over factual accuracy
([Casper et al., 2023](#bib.bib57); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib55);
[Gekhman et al., 2024](#bib.bib56)). Consequently, Reinforcement
Learning (RL) has become a necessity for optimizing LLMs towards more
truthfulness ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib58); [Gemma,
2025](#bib.bib73)). However, the standard outcome-level RL rewards lack
the granularity required to supervise fine-grained factual consistency,
leading to a fundamental misalignment between the scalar reward and the
nuanced evidentiary requirements of RAG. Specifically, Reinforcement
Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) ([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib2))
typically relies on reward models (RMs) ([Bradley and Terry,
1952](#bib.bib5); [Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib84); [Li et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib85); [Liu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib4)) that compress
multifaceted evaluations into coarse-grained scalar scores. This loss of
granularity limits the ability to verify individual claims, providing
insufficient signals to reinforce the meticulous evidentiary grounding
required for data-intensive tasks. Alternatively, while Reinforcement
Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib6))
attempts to provide objective feedback via deterministic rules ([Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib3)), rubrics ([Gunjal et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)), or
external generalist reward model ([Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib41)), it
remains fundamentally constrained by a dual-dependency bottleneck: the
scarcity of expert-annotated groundtruth in specialized domains, and the
reasoning ceilings of external verifiers. Consequently, unsupported
intermediate claims can persist, as models are rewarded for correct
final outcomes despite potentially hallucinated reasoning trajectories
([Li and Ng, 2025](#bib.bib75)).

While post-hoc metrics and fact-checkers ([Tang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib45); [Rashkin et al., 2023](#bib.bib40); [Gao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib44); [Baker et al., 2025](#bib.bib86); [Guan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87)) provide utility for evaluation, such static tools are
seldom integrated into the internal optimization loop to provide
actionable, claim-oriented guidance. More critically, the efficacy of
such verifiers is fundamentally undermined by the information leakage
inherent in current evaluation schemes ([Seo et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)).
Specifically, concurrent exposure to the query, documents, and generated
response induces a confirmation bias ([Sharma et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)). In this state, verifiers tend to prioritize
validating internal coherence over objective grounding against source
evidence, leading to the unwarranted endorsement of erroneous claims.
This compromised “blind scrutiny” prevents the model from internalizing
the rigorous, document-anchored reasoning essential for high-fidelity
generation.

To address above factuality challenges, we introduce Multi-Agent
Reinforced self-Check for Hallucination (MARCH), an RL-based framework
that enforces factual alignment through deliberate information
asymmetry. MARCH orchestrates a collaborative pipeline of three
specialized agents: a Solver, a Proposer, and a Checker, to prevent
model-based verifiers from taking cognitive shortcuts through
confirmation bias. As illustrated in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
the Solver first generates a response based on the query and retrieved
documents. Subsequently, the Proposer acts as a ’Response Atomizer,’
deconstructing the narrative into discrete, verifiable claims. Finally,
the Checker validates these claims by re-answering them exclusively
based on the source documents, strictly blinded to the Solver’s original
output to avoid cognitive contamination. Through this asymmetric
decoupling, MARCH transforms the verification process from a circular
confirmation of plausible text into a rigorous cross-examination between
generated claims and factual evidence. During training, MARCH promotes
agentic self-evolution via a zero-tolerance reward mechanism: any
discrepancy between the Proposer’s extracted claims and the Checker’s
document-based validation triggers a penalty on the entire response
trajectory. This encourages the agents to align their outputs strictly
with retrieved evidence, effectively internalizing the capability for
rigorous, document-anchored statements. Experimentally, MARCH achieves a
substantial reduction in hallucinations compared to its base model,
without requiring additional human annotations or external fact-checking
tools, thereby demonstrating the efficacy of our asymmetric
collaborative reinforcement paradigm. Notably, an 8B-parameter LLM
equipped with MARCH achieves performance parity with leading
closed-source models on multiple hallucination benchmarks, while
simultaneously delivering significant gains in general RAG-QA tasks.
These results establish a scalable and verifiable pathway toward
trustworthy, agentic self-improvement for large language models.

## 2 Methodology

### 2.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

Given an input query $`{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}`$ and a set of retrieved
documents $`{\bm{D}}=[{\bm{d}}_{1},{\bm{d}}_{2},\dots,{\bm{d}}_{l}]`$,
we aim to optimize a policy model
$`\pi_{\theta}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})`$ that generates a response
$`{\bm{y}}`$ with maximum factual grounding aligned with the provided
evidences in $`{\bm{D}}`$. Formally, suppose we can extract all the
statements of facts $`\{{\bm{a}}_{1},{\bm{a}}_{2},\dots,{\bm{a}}_{n}\}`$
from the response $`{\bm{y}}`$ using a function
$`{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot)`$, as
$`{\mathcal{A}}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{a}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$. Then, from the
perspective of reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), if
an oracle set of ground-truth annotations
$`\mathcal{A}^{*}=\{{\bm{a}}^{*}_{1},\dots,{\bm{a}}^{*}_{n}\}`$ is
ideally available for every atomic statement $`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$ in
$`{\bm{y}}`$, the optimization objective is to maximize the expected
evidentiary consistency:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim{\mathcal{X}},{\bm{y}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})}[R(\{{\bm{a}}_{i},{\bm{a}}^{*}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})],
``` |  | (1) |

where $`R(\cdot)`$ is a fact-check function that identifies the exact
match between $`\mathcal{A}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{a}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ and
$`\{{\bm{a}}^{*}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$. However, $`\mathcal{A}^{*}`$ is
practically unavailable in most application domains and requires
enormous human annotation.

Therefore, we reformulate equation
[1](#S2.E1 "In 2.1 Problem Formulation and Overview ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
into a self-contained, verifiable objective by decomposing the grounding
process into three separate agent tasks, as illustrated in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"):

1.  1.
    Response Generation: a Solver agent ordinarily responses
    $`{\bm{y}}`$ based on the input query $`{\bm{x}}`$ and retrieved
    context $`{\bm{D}}`$.
2.  2.
    Claim-level QA Proposal: a Proposer agent decomposes the response
    $`{\bm{y}}`$ into $`n`$ discrete factual claims in a
    question-answering (QA) format, as
    $`{\mathcal{Q}}({\bm{y}})=\{({\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{a}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}`$.
3.  3.
    Factual Verification: a Checker agent answers all the atomic
    questions $`\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ as
    $`\{\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ with only the retrieval
    documents $`{\bm{D}}`$ provided, without any access to the original
    response $`{\bm{y}}`$ and extracted
    answers$`\{{\bm{a}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$.

By substituting the unreachable oracle $`{\bm{a}}^{*}_{i}`$ with the
grounding result $`\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}`$ from the multi-agent pipeline,
we approximate the factuality optimization as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim{\mathcal{X}},{\bm{y}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})}\left[R(\{({\bm{a}}_{i},\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})\right].
``` |  | (2) |

By optimizing equation
[2](#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Problem Formulation and Overview ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
we force $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to internalize a rigorous verification logic,
ensuring that the generated content is strictly anchored in the source
evidence to enhance overall factual accuracy. We call the proposed
learning scheme Multi-Agent Reinforced self-Check for Hallucination
(MARCH).

### 2.2 MARCH Modeling

As shown in Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
we instantiate the functional primitives identified above into three
specialized agents derived from the same base policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$: a
Solver, a Proposer, and a Checker, which are conditioned to exhibit
distinct epistemic behaviors, effectively transforming the RAG task into
a structured, asymmetric cooperative game. MARCH begins with the
Solver’s policy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nu_{\text{solve}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{solve}}),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`{\bm{s}}_{\text{solve}}`$ is the Solver’s system prompt (as
shown in Appendix
[A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 System Prompt of the Solver Agent ‣ Appendix A Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"))
to induce the policy model $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to generate a comprehensive
response $`{\bm{y}}`$ given the retrieval documents $`{\bm{D}}`$ and the
input $`{\bm{x}}`$.

To decouple the continuous response $`{\bm{y}}`$ into verifiable
components, the Proposer agent functions as a Response Atomizer that
bridges narrative synthesis and discrete verification:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nu_{\text{propose}}(\cdot|{\bm{y}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{y}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{propose}}),
``` |  | (4) |

where the Propser’s system prompt $`{\bm{s}}_{\text{propose}}`$ is in
Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 System Prompt of the Proposer Agent ‣ Appendix A Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").
Specifically, $`\nu_{\text{propose}}`$ decomposes the response
$`{\bm{y}}`$ into a set of $`n`$ self-contained factual question-answer
(QA) pairs
$`\mathcal{Q}({\bm{\tau}})=\{({\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{a}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}`$,
where each $`{\bm{q}}_{i}`$ represents a targeted inquiry, and each
$`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$ denotes the corresponding claim asserted in
$`{\bm{y}}`$. The function $`{\mathcal{Q}}(\cdot)`$ extracts the QA
pairs from the Proposer’s generation
$`{\bm{\tau}}\sim\nu_{\text{propose}}(\cdot|{\bm{y}})`$. the Checker
operates as the Blinded Auditor and the linchpin of the asymmetric
cooperation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nu_{\text{check}}(\cdot|\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},{\bm{D}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\},{\bm{D}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{check}})
``` |  | (5) |

with the Checker’s prompt $`{\bm{s}}_{\text{check}}`$ in Appendix
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 System Prompt of the Checker Agent ‣ Appendix A Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
To eliminate confirmation bias and break information symmetry, when
tasked with answering $`{\bm{q}}_{i}`$, $`\nu_{\text{check}}`$ is
strictly blinded to the Solver’s response $`{\bm{y}}`$ and the
corresponding claims $`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$. the Checker replies all the
queries $`\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ in a response
$`\bm{\lambda}\sim\nu_{\text{check}}(\cdot|\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},{\bm{D}})`$,
only based on the RAG documents $`{\bm{D}}`$. The corresponding answers
$`{\mathcal{A}}(\bm{\lambda})=\{\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ are
parsed by the function $`{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot)`$ to serve as the
re-checked answers to the QA pairs
$`\{({\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{a}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}`$.

##### Overall Objective.

By integrating the conditional dependencies of the Solver, the Proposer,
and the Checker, MARCH defines a unified asymmetric cooperative and play
objective by focusing on the evidentiary identity between Solver’s
response $`{\bm{y}}`$ and Checker’s independent grounding trajectory
$`\bm{\lambda}`$, mediated by the atomic claim decomposition of the
Proposer. The optimization goal is to maximize the expected reward based
on the consistency of claims, marginalized over the discrete atomization
performed by $`\nu_{\text{propose}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\ \mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim{\mathcal{X}},{\bm{y}}\sim\nu_{\text{solve}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})}\left[R(\{({\bm{a}}_{i},\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})\right]`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t. }\{({\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{a}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}={\mathcal{Q}}({\bm{\tau}})`$ | $`\displaystyle,\ {\bm{\tau}}\sim\nu_{\text{propose}}(\cdot|{\bm{y}})\{\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}={\mathcal{A}}(\bm{\lambda}),\ \bm{\lambda}\sim\nu_{\text{check}}(\cdot|\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},{\bm{D}})`$ |  |  |

where $`R(\cdot)`$ measures the evidentiary identity between each
asserted claim $`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$ and the independent grounding
$`\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}`$. By optimizing equation
[6](#S2.E6 "In Overall Objective. ‣ 2.2 MARCH Modeling ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
the policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is compelled to internalize a rigorous
verification logic, ensuring that its narrative synthesis is strictly
anchored in verifiable evidence to enhance overall factual accuracy,
which also develops a self-consistent grounding capability that
eliminates reliance on external supervision.

### 2.3 MARCH Implementation

In our implementation, we specifically prioritize numerical and
quantitative verification, driven by the observation that in
data-intensive RAG scenarios, LLMs frequently suffer from hallucinations
such as misquoting figures or altering numerical values during context
integration. By anchoring the verification loop on these high-fidelity
tokens, MARCH provides a more rigorous evidentiary baseline for
grounding long-form reasoning.

##### Zero-Tolerance Reward (ZTR).

To enforce absolute factual grounding, we define a binary Zero-Tolerance
Reward function $`R(\{({\bm{a}}_{i},\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})`$
in equation
[6](#S2.E6 "In Overall Objective. ‣ 2.2 MARCH Modeling ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").
In the RAG context, we posit that any single hallucinated claim
$`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$ within the response $`{\bm{y}}`$ invalidates the entire
reasoning chain. Therefore, a trajectory is assigned a successful score
only if every claim $`{\bm{a}}_{i}`$ asserted by the Solver achieves an
identity match with the consensus answer $`\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}`$
extracted by the Checker:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R(\{({\bm{a}}_{i},\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n})=\begin{cases}0,\hskip-6.45831pt&\text{if every }{\bm{a}}_{i}=\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}\\
-1,\hskip-6.45831pt&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
``` |  | (7) |

This “all-or-nothing” reward structure prevents the policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ from optimizing for partial correctness or stylistic
plausibility, forcing the model to prioritize strict evidentiary
identity. Besides, to ensure the Checker provides a reliable baseline
for the audit and to reduce the variance of the reward signal, we employ
a multi-sampling strategy during the cross-validation phase. For each
question $`{\bm{q}}_{i}`$ generated by the Proposer,
$`\nu_{\text{check}}`$ generates multiple independent audit
trajectories. We apply a majority voting to determine the final
consensus answer $`\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i}`$, which effectively mitigates
stochastic errors in Checker’s generation in one independent audit.

##### Policy Optimization.

We optimize the shared policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ of the three agents using
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib1)).
Critically, we incorporate both the reasoning path $`{\bm{y}}`$ and the
audit trajectory
$`\bm{\lambda}\sim\nu_{\text{check}}(\cdot|\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\},{\bm{D}})`$
into the optimization loop, ensuring that $`\pi_{\theta}`$ concurrently
evolves as both a reliable generator and a rigorous auditor.
Consequently, each original query of a training batch
$`{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathcal{B}`$ contributes two distinct reward signals
to the policy, allowing $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to learn the fine-grained
correspondence between narrative synthesis and independent
document-grounding within a unified training batch. While both
trajectories derive their terminal reward from the same evidentiary
identity match (equation
[7](#S2.E7 "In Zero-Tolerance Reward (ZTR). ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")),
corresponding advantages $`\hat{A}`$ and KL-divergence ([Csiszár,
1975](#bib.bib10)) penalties against the reference model
$`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$ are estimated independently. The joint gradient is
computed as the sum of gradients across all individual trajectories
$`\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{MARCH}}(\theta)\approx`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{2|{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{B}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\hat{A}_{y}^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}({y}^{t}|\cdot)+\sum_{t=1}^{|\bm{\lambda}|}\hat{A}_{\lambda}^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}({\lambda}^{t}|*)-\beta\nabla_{\theta}\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]\Bigg]`$ |  | (8) |

where $`\hat{A}_{\lambda}^{t}`$ and $`\hat{A}_{y}^{t}`$ are the $`t`$-th
token’s corresponding advantages of the Checker’s output
$`\bm{\lambda}`$ and the Solver’s output $`{\bm{y}}`$, estimated via
Generalized Advantage Estimation ([Schulman et al., 2015](#bib.bib43)).
The notation $`(\cdot)`$ and $`(*)`$ in equation
[8](#S2.E8 "In Policy Optimization. ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
encapsulates the respective contexts for brevity:
$`({\bm{x}},{\bm{D}},{\bm{y}}^{<t})`$ and
$`(\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\},{\bm{D}},\bm{\lambda}^{<t})`$ for the Solver’s and
the Checker’s generation prefixes. equation
[8](#S2.E8 "In Policy Optimization. ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
ensures that $`\pi_{\theta}`$ concurrently refines its narrative
generation and evidentiary precision, internalizing a self-contained
verification loop where generative assertions are inherently tethered to
the policy’s own auditing capacity. We summarize our training algorithm
in Algorithm
[1](#algorithm1 "In Policy Optimization. ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").

1 Input: An LLM Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$; A Training Batch
$`\mathcal{B}=\{({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{D}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{B}|}`$;
Solver, Proposer and Checker System Prompts
$`\{{\bm{s}}_{\text{solve}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{propose}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{check}}\}`$;

// Phase 1: Multi-Agent Collaboration and Rollout

2 for *each training sample $`({\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})\in\mathcal{B}`$* do

   // Step 1: Generate reasoning path $`{\bm{y}}`$ from Solver

    3 Sample
$`{\bm{y}}\sim\nu_{\text{solve}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},{\bm{D}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{solve}})`$;

   // Step 2: Atomize response $`{\bm{y}}`$ by Proposer and Parse QA
pairs by $`\mathcal{Q}(\cdot)`$

    4 Sample
$`\bm{\tau}\sim\nu_{\text{propose}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{y}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{y}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{propose}})`$;

    5 Extract QA pairs
$`\{({\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{a}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}=\mathcal{Q}(\bm{\tau})`$;

   // Step 3: Generate audit trajectory $`\bm{\lambda}`$ from Checker
and Parse re-checked answers by $`\mathcal{A}(\cdot)`$

    6 Sample
$`\bm{\lambda}\sim\nu_{\text{check}}(\cdot\mid\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},{\bm{D}})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},{\bm{D}},{\bm{s}}_{\text{check}})`$;

    7 Parse re-checked answers
$`\{(\hat{{\bm{a}}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}=\mathcal{A}(\bm{\lambda})`$;

   // Step 4: Unified reward labeling

    8 Calculate Zero-Tolerance Reward $`R_{i}`$ by equation
[7](#S2.E7 "In Zero-Tolerance Reward (ZTR). ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
(based on the match between $`{\bm{a}}`$ and $`\hat{{\bm{a}}}`$);

   // Step 5: Store both reasoning and auditing trajectories

    9 Add $`{\bm{y}}_{i}`$ and $`\bm{\lambda}_{i}`$ to the unified batch
trajectory set $`\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}}`$;

    10 Associate both $`{\bm{y}}_{i}`$ and $`\bm{\lambda}_{i}`$ with
terminal reward $`R_{i}`$;

11 end for

// Phase 2: Joint Policy Optimization

12 for *each trajectory
$`\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}}=\{{\bm{y}}_{i},\bm{\lambda}_{i}\}`$*
do

    13 Estimate Advantage $`\hat{A}_{\tau^{\prime}}`$ using GAE based on
$`R_{i}`$;

    14 Compute $`{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})`$ for each
token in $`\tau^{\prime}`$;

15 end for

16 Update $`\pi_{\theta}`$ by computing the joint gradient
$`\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{MARCH}}(\theta)`$ according to
equation
[8](#S2.E8 "In Policy Optimization. ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination") 
$`\frac{1}{2|{\mathcal{B}}|}\sum_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{B}}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\hat{A}_{y}^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}({y}^{t}|\cdot)+\sum_{t=1}^{|\bm{\lambda}|}\hat{A}_{\lambda}^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}({\lambda}^{t}|*)-\beta\nabla_{\theta}\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]\Bigg]`$;

17 where the notation $`(\cdot)`$ and $`(*)`$ in equation
[8](#S2.E8 "In Policy Optimization. ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
encapsulates the respective contexts for brevity:
$`({\bm{x}},{\bm{D}},{\bm{y}}^{<t})`$ and
$`(\{{\bm{q}}_{i}\},{\bm{D}},\bm{\lambda}^{<t})`$ for the Solver’s and
the Checker’s generation prefixes;

Algorithm 1 MARCH Training Process.

## 3 Experiment

We first evaluate the effectiveness of MARCH in mitigating
hallucinations. Then, we show that the improved factual consistency
ability helps downstream reasoning tasks like Question-Answering.

### 3.1 Training Setup

##### Training Datasets and Base Model.

We train our framework covering: a STEM
(Science-Technology-Engineering-Math) setting based on BioASQ ([Krithara
et al., 2023](#bib.bib20)), and a General setting based on
2WikiMultiHopQA ([Ho et al., 2020](#bib.bib21)) and MuSiQue ([Trivedi et
al., 2022](#bib.bib23)). Crucially, training is performed using only
queries and retrieved documents, without access to ground-truth answers
or annotations. Table
[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Datasets and Base Model. ‣ 3.1 Training Setup ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
shows the number of retrieved documents per query and the document
lengths vary widely across datasets, and a substantial fraction of the
documents are irrelevant to the query (e.g., 30.1% for STEM and up to
88.4% for MuSiQue). Such a high level of noise and heterogeneity in the
retrieval docs makes the training setting highly realistic but also
extremely challenging, as the agents must learn to perform
document-grounded fact checking in the presence of many noisy documents.
We consider Meta-Llama3.1-8B-Instruct ([Touvron et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7)) as the initialization policy.

| Dataset | Original Dataset | \#Samples | Avg. Query Len | \#Docs per Query |  |  | Total Doc Len (words) |  |  | Irrelevant Doc Ratio |
|  |  |  |  | Avg | Max | Min | Avg | Max | Min |  |
| STEM | BioASQ | 4721 | 8.62 | 9.03 | 157 | 1 | 1314.86 | 22135 | 1 | 30.14% |
| General | 2WikiMultiHopQA | 4500 | 12.87 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 575.65 | 2099 | 95 | 24.4% |

Table 1: Statistics of the training dataset, where we report the number
of training samples, average query length, the number of retrieved
documents per query, the average document length, and the proportion of
documents that are irrelevant to the query. The large variance in
document counts and lengths, together with the high ratio of irrelevant
documents, highlights the realism and difficulty of our training setup.

##### Training Details.

Training framework is built upon the VerL ([Sheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib76)), and we employ Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)
([Zhao et al., 2023](#bib.bib71)) for efficient multi-node multi-GPU
training. During the training rollout, we utilize the vLLM ([Kwon et
al., 2023](#bib.bib77)) for efficient sample generation with the
temperature of 0.6. The PPO ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib1))
training is conducted for a single epoch with a global batch size of 32,
with a max prompt length of 24,567, max response length of 8,192. We set
learning rates for the actor and the critic as $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ and
$`1\times 10^{-5}`$, respectively. We save and evaluate a checkpoint
every 20 steps, and report results from the single best-performing
checkpoint selected based on the highest average score across all
evaluation benchmarks. More detailed training hyper-parameters are in
Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Training Details ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").

### 3.2 Experiments on Hallucination

##### Evaluation Benchmark.

We evaluate MARCH along the aspect of *hallucination and factual
grounding* on the RAGTruth ([Niu et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)), FaithBench
([Tamber et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)), ContextualJudgeBench ([Xu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib19)) and Facts Grounding benchmark ([Jacovi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)), which cover QA, data-to-text writing, summarization,
and diverse domains such as medical, financial, and legal. Detailed
introductions are provided in Appendix
[B.2.1](#A2.SS2.SSS1 "B.2.1 Hallucination and Factual Grounding Benchmarks ‣ B.2 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").
The best performance is marked with Red and the second-best with Blue.

##### Evaluation Protocol and Metrics.

Following [Niu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib16); [Tamber et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib18); [Jacovi et al. (2025)](#bib.bib17); [Xu et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib19), we focus on *response-level* factuality eval.
Given generation, retrieved documents, and ground-truth reference, we
deploy a Qwen3-235B-A22B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)) as a judge
model to decide whether the response is factually consistent/accurate
with the evidence/ground-truth factual labels. We mitigate the
randomness during evaluation by drawing eight independent generations
for each test query; the judge model then evaluates each sampling
individually, and the final verdict is determined by a majority vote
across these eight trajectories.

##### Results on RAGTruth and FaithBench.

Table
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Results on RAGTruth and FaithBench. ‣ 3.2 Experiments on Hallucination ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
shows that our method brings substantial and consistent improvements
over the base Llama3.1-8B-Instruct across all settings. With STEM data
(MARCH-STEM), the learned policy improves the average accuracy from
55.20 to 74.93 (+19.73) and with General QA data (MARCH-General), the
average accuracy further rises to 75.23 (+20.03), which suggest that
MARCH reliably strengthens the base model’s ability to judge and
mitigate hallucinations, rather than overfitting to a particular domain.
When compared to other larger or proprietary LLMs, our policies also
achieve an advanced average performance. Together, these results
demonstrate that our framework can turn a small-sized base LLM into a
highly competitive factuality judge simply by training on noisy,
document-grounded RAG data.

##### Results on Facts Grounding.

FACTS Grounding evaluates whether model responses are fully supported by
a single source document. Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Results on Facts Grounding. ‣ 3.2 Experiments on Hallucination ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
shows that our policies achieve large gains over the base model,
reaching a factuality score of 85.23% (MARCH-STEM) and 80.12%
(MARCH-General), compared with 57.09% for the base Llama3.1-8B-Instruct.
Our method successfully lifts an 8B backbone into the comparable
performance band as leading proprietary models, placing MARCH-STEM just
behind the top Gemini 2.5/1.5 Flash models on the public leaderboard
while surpassing popular models such as GPT-4o and several larger open
models. The strong results indicate that MARCH substantially improves
long-document grounding robustness across heterogeneous domains.

##### Results on ContextualJudgeBench.

Table
[3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Results on Facts Grounding. ‣ 3.2 Experiments on Hallucination ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
reports results on ContextualJudgeBench, which evaluates multiple
dimensions of judge behavior, including refusal, faithfulness,
completeness, and conciseness. Starting from Llama3.1-8B, our framework
again yields large gains across all eight dimensions under both training
regimes. Specifically, the policy trained on General QA data
(MARCH-General) improves the average accuracy from 29.7 to 51.6 (+21.9),
while the policy trained on STEM data (MARCH-STEM) reaches 52.3 (+22.6).
The improvements are particularly pronounced on faithfulness and
completeness (both QA and summarization), where accurate
document-grounded judgment is most critical. Based on an 8B LLM, our
policies surprisingly reach or surpass the performance of many much
larger judge models, and approach the best specialized judge models on
several dimensions. Table
[3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Results on Facts Grounding. ‣ 3.2 Experiments on Hallucination ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
indicates that MARCH not only improves binary hallucination detection
but also equips LLM with a more nuanced ability to assess answer quality
along multiple axes, such as whether key information is covered and
whether responses remain concise and well-calibrated in context.

### 3.3 Experiments on Multi-Hop QA

Intuitively, the capacity for precise factual extraction and
verification reasonably serves as the fundamental bedrock for complex
reasoning, as Question Answering tasks usually require a model to
sequentially bridge information across disparate documents. In this
section, we empirically find that the improved factual grounding brought
by MARCH can directly translate into better performance on
reasoning-intensive downstream tasks.

##### Evaluation Benchmarks.

Following [Xu et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib47); [Trivedi et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib46); [Shao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib48), we evaluate the
performance of our MARCH on three popular multi-hop QA datasets,
including HotpotQA ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib22)), 2WikiMultiHopQA
([Ho et al., 2020](#bib.bib21)) and MuSiQue ([Trivedi et al.,
2022](#bib.bib23)). More details about datasets are provided in Appendix
[B.2.2](#A2.SS2.SSS2 "B.2.2 QA Benchmarks ‣ B.2 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").

##### Evaluation Protocol and Metrics.

Following [Xu et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib47); [Shao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib48); [Trivedi et al. (2023)](#bib.bib46), we sample the
first 500 examples from the development set of each dataset as our
evaluation subset to reduce the evaluation overhead while maintaining
statistical reliability. For each question, the model receives the query
and its associated context passages and produces a corresponding answer.
We report accuracy (%) with respect to the GT reference answers judged
by a Qwen3-235B-A22B, using the official evaluation scripts when
available. We also draw eight independent generations for each test
query and then adopt a majority voting to decide the final verdict.

##### Comparison with Existing Baselines.

Table
[4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. ‣ 3.3 Experiments on Multi-Hop QA ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
compares MARCH-Best, which incorporates joint optimization of both the
Solver and the Checker alongside CoT prompting, with various specialized
RAG methods and proprietary models. Within the 8B-parameter scale, MARCH
achieves higher accuracy on the HotpotQA and MuSiQue benchmarks compared
to methods such as RAFT ([Dong et al., 2023](#bib.bib50)) and GenGround
([Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib49)). Notably, on the HotpotQA benchmark,
which contains a high density of noisy documents, MARCH reaches an
accuracy of 71.2%, exceeding the reported results of standard GPT-4o RAG
(64.0%) and the IRCoT ([Trivedi et al., 2023](#bib.bib46)) framework
using GPT-4o (66.4%). Table
[4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. ‣ 3.3 Experiments on Multi-Hop QA ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
suggests that MARCH can effectively enhance the factual reliability of
smaller models in multi-hop reasoning scenarios, leading to performance
that is comparable to and even higher than much larger proprietary
models.

### 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation

##### Performance Analysis of Joint Optimization.

Table
[5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Does our method conflict with other boosting methods? ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
illustrates that the joint optimization of the Solver and the Checker
consistently achieves the highest accuracy across all training
strategies in both STEM and General benchmarks. A key observation is
that while the Solver-only update provides a base improvement, the
inclusion of the Checker significantly amplifies the model’s reasoning
capabilities, particularly in complex scenarios. Specifically, in the
Few-Shot setting for STEM, the joint model achieves a remarkable
absolute gain of 11.6% over the Solver-only version. These results
suggest that the Checker’s auditing signal is crucial for leveraging the
full potential of advanced prompting techniques like few-shot and CoT,
as it effectively mitigates factual drift and ensures logical
consistency throughout multi-hop reasoning trajectories. In summary,
Table
[5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Does our method conflict with other boosting methods? ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
suggests that by internalizing a claim-level auditing logic, MARCH
significantly amplifies the efficacy of in-context learning and
multi-step reasoning, ensuring that increased model capacity translates
into verifiable factual accuracy rather than hallucinated complexity.

##### Does our method conflict with other boosting methods?

As demonstrated in Table
[5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Does our method conflict with other boosting methods? ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
MARCH is highly orthogonal and can be seamlessly integrated with
existing performance-boosting techniques, including RLHF, Few-Shot
prompting, and CoT reasoning. When applied to the Llama3.1-8B-Instruct
baseline, our method consistently achieves significant performance gains
across all benchmarks. For instance, combining MARCH with CoT reasoning
further elevates the average accuracy on STEM tasks from 50.93% to
59.13%, and on General tasks from 51.00% to 57.80%. Similarly, notable
improvements are observed when MARCH is integrated with Few-Shot
(10-Shots) configurations, reaching an average of 61.27% on STEM. Table
[5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Does our method conflict with other boosting methods? ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
indicates that MARCH does not conflict with traditional scaling or
prompting methods; rather, it provides a complementary layer of factual
rigor through its asymmetric self-play mechanism, leading to a
cumulative enhancement in multi-hop question-answering capabilities. We
provide the implementation details in Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Baseline Methods ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").

two training datasets based on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct. We report the
accuracy rate (%) by comparing the model output with the corresponding
ground-truth label. We produce baseline results on our own environment.

##### Influence of Reward Formulations.

We evaluate two reward formulations: (i) Error Rate Reward (ERR), a
proportional penalty based on the ratio of incorrect claims, which is
defined as $`R_{\text{ERR}}=-\frac{N_{\text{err}}}{N_{\text{total}}}`$,
where $`N_{\text{total}}`$ is the total number of claims generated and
$`N_{\text{err}}`$ is the number of claims identified as incorrect by
the Checker. and (ii) Zero-Tolerance Reward (ZTR), the binary constraint
that enforces absolute consistency defined in equation
[7](#S2.E7 "In Zero-Tolerance Reward (ZTR). ‣ 2.3 MARCH Implementation ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination").
As shown in Table
[6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Performance on Different Model Family. ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
while all RL-tuned configurations significantly outperform the vanilla
baselines, ZTR consistently surpasses ERR (e.g., 61.25% vs 55.46% on
Llama3.1 joint-training), suggesting that strict logical consistency is
more effective for complex RAG tasks. Within the ZTR, the penalty-based
scalar ($`-1/0`$) yields superior results compared to the
incentive-based ($`0/1`$) setting, as the former provides a stronger
corrective gradient to suppress hallucinations.

##### Impact of Reward Scalars

We further compare two scalar assignments within the ZTR framework: a
penalty-based setting ($`-1/0`$) and an incentive-based setting
($`0/1`$). The second group in Table
[6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Performance on Different Model Family. ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")
on the STEM dataset show that the $`-1/0`$ configuration (59.06%)
significantly outperforms the $`0/1`$ setting (50.42%). We hypothesize
that because factual successes are relatively sparse during early
training phases, the $`0/1`$ incentive fails to provide sufficient
contrast between diverse erroneous paths. In contrast, the $`-1/0`$
setting establishes factual accuracy as the default expectation,
providing a robust corrective gradient that effectively suppresses
hallucinations.

##### Performance on Different Model Family.

As shown in the last group in Table
[6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Performance on Different Model Family. ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study and Further Investigation ‣ 3 Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
the MARCH framework exhibits robust generalizability across different
model families, with Qwen3-8B reflecting the same performance trajectory
observed in Llama-based experiments. Specifically, MARCH elevates
Qwen3-8B to average accuracies of 67.90% and 68.11% under General and
STEM settings, respectively, marking a significant absolute gain of over
11% compared to its vanilla baseline (56.84%) and demonstrating that the
dual-trajectory optimization mechanism is model-agnostic and
consistently internalizes superior evidentiary grounding across diverse
architectures.

## 4 Related Work

##### Hallucinations and Fact-Check in RAG.

While RAG reduces fabrications by anchoring responses in external
context ([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib14)), LLMs remain susceptible to
context-conflicting hallucinations ([Shuster et al., 2021](#bib.bib67)).
Current mitigation efforts largely revolve around outcome-level
supervision ([Shi et al., 2023](#bib.bib65); [Gekhman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib56); [Yu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib64); [Asai et al.,
2023](#bib.bib63)), post-hoc reasoning refinements and utilizing
external verifiers to filter outputs during inference ([Dhuliawala et
al., 2023](#bib.bib70); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib69); [Min et al.,
2023](#bib.bib68); [Rashkin et al., 2023](#bib.bib40); [Gao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib44); [Tang et al., 2024](#bib.bib45)). However, these
methods often treat LLM as a black box and fail to internalize factual
constraints within the training objective itself. Moving beyond, we
propose a framework where the model learns to prioritize factual
adherence by minimizing logical discrepancies identified through an
internal audit.

##### Multi-Agent Systems for LLMs.

Multi-agent systems have emerged as a robust paradigm for enhancing LLM
performance through collaborative or adversarial interactions ([Du et
al., 2023](#bib.bib38); [Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)), which typically
assign distinct personas to one / multiple model instances to facilitate
code generation ([Huang et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Islam et al.,
2024](#bib.bib30)), complex reasoning ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib36);
[He et al., 2023](#bib.bib35); [Talebirad and Nadiri,
2023](#bib.bib37)), decision-making ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib31);
[Yu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib32)), recommendation ([Wang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib34)), and debate-driven consensus ([Du et al.,
2023](#bib.bib38); [Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)). While effective at
inference time, most existing architectures treat agents as separate
entities, often overlooking the potential for joint policy optimization
across different functional roles. In addition, previous work shows that
multi-agent system sometimes amplifies the hallucination of LLMs ([Hong
et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)). Our framework differs by instantiating
functionally distinct roles within a single shared policy. By
structurally enforcing an information barrier between agents, we
facilitate the co-evolution of generative and evaluative capabilities
within a unified training loop, ensuring that the model’s internal
verification logic directly informs its generative precision.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced MARCH, a multi-agent framework designed to
mitigate hallucinations in data-intensive RAG tasks. By reconfiguring a
shared policy into a coordinated hierarchy comprising a Solver, a
Proposer, and a Checker, MARCH enables LLMs to simultaneously refine
their synthesis reasoning and independent grounding capabilities. Our
experiments demonstrate that the combination of a Zero-Tolerance Reward
mechanism and dual-trajectory PPO effectively internalizes a
self-contained verification loop, consistently outperforming strong
baselines. The robust generalization of MARCH across diverse model
families underscores its potential as a scalable, high-fidelity solution
for information synthesis in complex knowledge domains. We believe this
agentic co-evolution paradigm offers a promising pathway toward building
inherently trustworthy and verifiable large language models.

### B.2 Evaluation Details

#### B.2.1 Hallucination and Factual Grounding Benchmarks

##### RAGTruth and FaithBench

are public benchmarks for evaluating hallucinations in
retrieval-augmented generation, which contain three task types: (i) QA,
(ii) Data2Txt Writing, and (iii) Summarization, each with
human-annotated hallucinations at the response level. For each example,
the model is given a query and a set of retrieved passages, and asked to
produce an answer, a data-to-text description, or a summary.

##### Contextual JudgeBench

is a judge benchmark with 2,000 challenging response pairs across eight
splits inspired by real-world contextual evaluation scenarios, which is
built with a multi-pronged data construction pipeline that leverages
both existing human annotations and model-based perturbations. The
evaluation task requires a model to act as a judge, choosing the better
of two provided responses (A and B) according to specific,
context-dependent criteria.

##### Facts Grounding

is a large-scale factuality benchmark spanning five domains (e.g.,
medical, financial, legal, and others) and nine task types, including
summarization, fact finding, comparison, and definition. Each instance
consists of a query, a collection of documents, and a reference output
with fine-grained factual annotations, providing a broad and challenging
testbed for document-grounded evaluation. During test, we adopt the
official JSON judgment prompt provided by [Jacovi et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib17).

#### B.2.2 QA Benchmarks

##### HotpotQA.

HotpotQA ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib22)) is a large-scale multi-hop QA
dataset that requires reasoning over multiple Wikipedia passages to
answer fact-based questions. Each question is paired with multiple
supporting paragraphs and a short, factoid-style answer.

##### 2WikiMultiHopQA.

2WikiMultiHopQA ([Ho et al., 2020](#bib.bib21)) extends HotpotQA with
questions that require reasoning across two different Wikipedia
articles, emphasizing cross-document retrieval and multi-hop reasoning
over disjoint evidence.

##### MuSiQue.

MuSiQue ([Trivedi et al., 2022](#bib.bib23)) is a challenging multi-hop
QA dataset with questions that explicitly require reasoning across
multiple sentences scattered across different documents, often involving
compositional reasoning over several intermediate facts.

### B.3 Baseline Methods

##### Baselines.

The raw backbone model used in all settings, evaluated in a zero-shot
manner with task-specific instructions but without additional reasoning
or RL fine-tuning.

##### +CoT.

A prompting baseline where we encourage step-by-step reasoning by
prepending chain-of-thought instructions (e.g., “let’s think step by
step”) to the prompt. The model is still the same base LLM; only the
decoding prompt is changed.

##### +Few-Shot.

An in-context learning baseline where we augment the prompt with a small
number of annotated QA examples (few-shot demonstrations) drawn from the
training distribution, following standard practice in multi-hop QA and
factuality evaluation.

##### +RLHF.

A version of the base LLM further optimized with reinforcement learning
from human feedback, using general-purpose reward models that favor
helpful and harmless responses but are not specifically tuned for
document-grounded factuality. We adopt Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B
([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib54)) as the reward model.

### B.4 How Would Proposed Question Numbers Influence Performance?

A potential reward hacking of the MARCH framework could be that the
system may attempt to inflate its reward by reducing the number of
proposed questions, adhering to a “less said, less leaked” strategy
where fewer claims minimize the probability of being audited as a
hallucination. As illustrated in Figure
[3](#A2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ B.4 How Would Proposed Question Numbers Influence Performance? ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
we indeed observe a gradual decline in the average number of proposed
questions as training progresses across all configurations. Notably, the
configuration involving joint updates of the Solver + Checker exhibits a
more pronounced downward trend compared to the Solver Only baseline,
suggesting that the zero-tolerance penalty on the Checker’s trajectory
imposes a stricter consistency bottleneck, further incentivizing the
Proposer to prune potentially risky claims.

However, we find that this quantitative shrinkage can be effectively
mitigated through simple instructional constraints. By explicitly
requiring the Proposer to generate no fewer than $`k`$ questions within
the prompt (e.g., $`k=3`$), the decline in question density is
significantly arrested. As shown by the solid lines in Figure
[3](#A2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ B.4 How Would Proposed Question Numbers Influence Performance? ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination"),
models with such constraints in the legend (solid lines marked with “w/
constraint”) maintain a much more stable and higher volume of factual
inquiries throughout the self-evolution process, which indicates that
the MARCH framework remains robust when balanced with basic
task-specific instructions, ensuring that the drive for factual accuracy
does not come at the cost of informational density.

Figure 3: Average number of proposed questions per step on the STEM
training dataset. The dashed lines represent the MARCH framework without
maintaining the question number, while the solid lines (w/ Constraint)
indicate the results after incorporating instructional constraints to
maintain informational density.

### B.5 Visualization of Training Dynamics and Time Consuming

To further investigate the practical efficiency of the MARCH framework,
we analyze the training dynamics and computational overhead. Figures
[4](#A2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ B.5 Visualization of Training Dynamics and Time Consuming ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")(a)-(d)
illustrate the stable convergence of accuracy and rewards across both
General and STEM datasets, where the joint Solver + Checker update
consistently outperforms the Solver Only configuration. Regarding
training efficiency, Figure
[4](#A2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ B.5 Visualization of Training Dynamics and Time Consuming ‣ Appendix B Experiment ‣ MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination")(e)
presents the cumulative time consumption on the General dataset
(containing 9,000 samples), where we find that simultaneously updating
both the Solver and the Checker trajectories in a single training step
does not impose a prohibitive computational burden.

Figure 4: Visualization of training efficiency and dynamics. (a)-(d)
illustrate the convergence of accuracy and rewards across general and
STEM datasets. (e) Comparison of cumulative training time on the General
dataset.
````
